beats.text: Week six builds a model out of tiny units. Each one does the simplest thing there is: multiply, then add.
This is a perceptron. Inputs x one and x two come in, and every connection has a weight.
Multiply each input by its weight, add them up, and that sum is the output.
There is one more input, x zero, which is always one. Its weight, w zero, is the bias.
The slides write all of this as w transpose x. So what does transpose mean?
In the slides, vectors are columns. Transpose turns a column into a row. Here, w is minus one point five, one, and one.
A row times a column pairs the entries: first with first, second with second, third with third. Multiply each pair.
Add the products. Minus one point five, plus one, plus one, is zero point five. A row times a column is always one number: the weighted sum.
So why do we need the bias?
For regression, the unit draws a line: y equals w x plus w zero. w sets the slope. w zero moves the whole line up or down.
Take the bias away, and every line must pass through the origin, whatever the data look like.
For classification, the unit outputs one when the sum is above zero. Keep both weights at one, and set the bias to minus one point five.
The boundary is the line x one plus x two equals one point five. Only the corner one, one is above it. That is AND.
Now change only the bias, to minus zero point five. The line slides down, and three corners are above it. That is OR.
Same weights, different bias. The weights choose the direction of the line. The bias chooses where it sits. That is bias shifting.
For the exam.
A perceptron outputs the weighted sum.
Transpose turns a column into a row.
w transpose x is one number.
Without a bias, the line must pass through the origin.
AND and OR differ only in the bias.
